spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The main move is to replace a finite real y-contour by a slanted ray and a vertical segment on which the cubic-linear phase becomes uniformly decaying. The lower bound on x and the smallness of cK1^2 turn an oscillatory integral into one that can be truncated at a nu-scale length, cut into unit intervals, and Taylor-compressed into a bounded family of polynomial moments coupled to F(K; a+alpha x,b).

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Lemma 5.4 introduces Ix(C), writes the target as an x-integral of Ix(C0)F, and uses Cauchy's theorem to express Ix(C0) through contours C1 and C2. Under 1/4 <= x and |cK1^2| < 1/48, both transformed integrands decay faster than exp(-y/6). Truncation at L=ceil(6 nu), unit-interval shifts, and Taylor expansion reduce the original integral, up to the stated small error, to O(nu^2) integrals of the two forms displayed in (5.20), which are referred to the earlier treatment of (5.9).
directed.conceptual_reading: Contour choice is doing computational compression: it converts nonstationarity into a uniform decay certificate, so the long continuous domain is forgotten after a controlled truncation and only finitely many local polynomial data remain. The lemma is therefore both an analytic reduction and a complexity certificate, not merely an existence argument.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge objects are Ix(C), the pair C1/C2, the exponential decay envelope, the truncation scale L, and the local Taylor polynomials. They connect the cubic y-phase to canonical x-integrals containing F(K; a+alpha x,b), returning the problem to the paper's established quadratic-sum interface.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The decay argument uses x bounded away from zero and a small cubic coefficient; it does not cover a stationary or near-zero x regime. The last evaluation is delegated to the earlier analysis after (5.9), so this span alone does not supply that terminal reduction or its constants. It proves an approximation and operation/bit bound under the lemma's parameter restrictions, not an unrestricted contour principle.
directed.uncertainty: The case architecture and decay/truncation mechanism are explicit in the span. Exact radicals, phase signs, and contour endpoints are formula-sensitive in the extracted text, and the definitions of nu, Lambda, F, and the earlier (5.9) evaluator lie outside this unit; no reconstruction of those details is assumed.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: This lemma builds a common evaluator by partitioning according to stationary geometry rather than forcing one expansion everywhere. Small beta is handled by localizing the x-variable and separating near- from far-coupling in y; large beta is handled by asking whether the x-stationary point lies inside the integration interval. Each branch is reshaped until the remaining object is an Airy-type cubic integral, with Gaussian completion used when a contour branch initially grows.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: For beta <= L, the proof rescales and subdivides x, Taylor-expands its quadratic factor, and splits y into I1 and I2 according to the size of |alpha1-theta y|. The near region permits expansion of the cross term after rescaling, while direct x-integration and inverse-power expansions treat the far region; both reduce to integrals (5.27). Those are evaluated by separating saddle and no-saddle cases, extracting a saddle contribution when present and otherwise shifting to a rapidly decaying contour, ultimately invoking incomplete Gamma evaluations. For beta >= L, I4 records when the x-stationary point lies in [0,w] and I5 when it does not. Vertical or diagonal contour replacements give decay off the stationary region. In the difficult I4 branch, complementary half-lines and a full Gaussian integral isolate the possible growth, and the full Gaussian again becomes an integral of form (5.27).
directed.conceptual_reading: The controlling abstraction is a geometry-aware case split: local Taylor compression is valid only after the relevant coupling is made small, while contour deformation is selected when separation from stationarity supplies decay. Saddle extraction, nonstationary deformation, and Gaussian completion are complementary representations of the same phase, chosen by where its critical point lies.
directed.representation_or_bridge: I1/I2 and I4/I5 are proof-relevant bridge objects because they encode frequency separation and stationary-point location. The normalized Airy-type family (5.27) is the shared intermediate representation reached from all branches; its saddle/no-saddle decomposition bridges the original double integral to rapidly truncated local integrals and incomplete Gamma functions. The tau1 and tau2 parameters expose how far the stationary point is from an endpoint.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The reduction depends on the stated bounds on beta, alpha, eta, c, and K1 and repeatedly imports procedures from Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Several steps are summarized as standard or requiring labor, so the span gives a complexity architecture rather than every local error estimate. The argument does not say that one Taylor expansion is uniformly valid across the stationary transition; the partitions are essential.
directed.uncertainty: The prose strongly supports the branch structure and the common reduction to (5.27). Exact square-root scalings, contour orientations, phase signs, and some displayed inequalities are typesetting-sensitive in the extracted artifact, so claims about those formulas are kept at the level explicitly stated. The referenced earlier Airy and incomplete-Gamma algorithms are not present in this unit.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The external x-contours are made cheap by a two-stage deformation. First the y-path is bent into cubic-decay directions and locally Taylor-compressed; then the x half-line is rotated according to the sign of the quadratic coefficient. When the rotated exponent initially grows, the half-line is represented as a full Gaussian minus a decaying complementary half-line, allowing explicit Gaussian integration and returning both pieces to quadratic exponential sums.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Lemma 5.6 shifts the positive external contour by 1/4 and deforms the y-segment into C1 and C2. On C1, small |c1 K1^2| gives exp(-y/16)-type decay, so y is truncated, subdivided, shifted, and Taylor-expanded to sums (5.38). The x-contour is then rotated to C3 or C4 according to the sign of alpha2. A lower bound on tau_k makes one half-line contribution decay after writing the problematic integral as a full-line Gaussian minus the negative half-line. The latter is truncated and expanded before incomplete-Gamma evaluation; explicit integration of the full Gaussian gives (5.46), whose short y-integral is Taylor-reduced. Both routes yield quadratic exponential sums handled by Theorem 2.1. The C2 branch is treated analogously using tilde-tau_k, and the negative external contour is identified as a conjugate case.
directed.conceptual_reading: The proof certifies that contour extensions introduced for saddle extraction do not create a new computational primitive. Decay removes most of the continuous tail, while Gaussian completion converts the remaining apparently unstable branch into an explicit bulk term plus a stable correction. The output representation closes back onto the same quadratic-sum evaluator used elsewhere.
directed.representation_or_bridge: C1/C2 expose decay in y, C3/C4 choose a stable direction for the quadratic x-phase, and tau_k or tilde-tau_k quantify separation across the summation range. The full-Gaussian-minus-half-line identity is the decisive bridge: the correction is reduced through incomplete Gamma integrals, while the full Gaussian produces a short y-integral and then quadratic exponential sums.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The certification requires alpha bounded away from zero at the stated Lambda scale, summation indices separated by a Lambda^2 margin, a nonzero controlled alpha2, and small c1K1^2. It relies on Theorem 2.1 and a previously established quadratic-sum class rather than deriving that evaluator here. Claims that certain n>0 terms are negligible and that C2 is analogous are stated in the proof but not expanded into independent estimates in this span.
directed.uncertainty: The qualitative deformations, decay logic, Gaussian split, and quadratic-sum endpoint are explicit. The extracted statement contains an ambiguous repeated alpha2/alpha2-style ratio and dense phase formulas whose superscripts, radicals, and signs may be OCR-sensitive; their exact intended algebra is therefore not reconstructed. The conclusion is conditional on the displayed hypotheses as typeset in the source.
